extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, IPR practitioners, patent owners, and appellate judges
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and legal principles governing Federal Circuit review of PTAB inter partes review decisions on patentability (anticipation/obviousness), claim construction, and procedural due process. Includes how factual findings and legal conclusions are reviewed and when reversal/vacatur/remand is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: APA/Agency action review standard
rubrics_metrics.description: We set aside the Board’s actions if they are 'arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion, or otherwise not in accordance with law,' or 'unsupported by substantial evidence.' 5 U.S.C. § 706(2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the governing standard for judicial review of PTAB decisions; legal questions are reviewed de novo while factual findings are reviewed for substantial evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of review: legal vs factual
rubrics_metrics.description: We review the Board’s legal decisions de novo and its factual determinations for substantial evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim construction and obviousness are treated as questions of law that depend on underlying factual findings, so courts review legal aspects de novo but underlying factual findings for substantial evidence (citing Teva; In re Brandt).

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial evidence definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Substantial evidence 'means such relevant evidence as a reasonable mind might accept as adequate to support a conclusion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to evaluate whether the Board's factual findings are supported; citation: Consol. Edison Co. v. N.L.R.B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipation is a question of fact, and a finding of anticipation requires that every limitation of the claim is present in a single prior art reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board must identify each claim limitation in a single prior reference (citing Ericsson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness: sufficiency when prior art sometimes meets claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Combinations of prior art that sometimes meet the claim elements are sufficient to show obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is enough that the combination would sometimes perform all the method steps (citing Unwired Planet and Hewlett‑Packard v. Mustek). Example: a prior-art system that would determine a claimed element 'some of the time' can teach that aspect of the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: No addition of unwritten claim limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: It is incorrect for the Board to read unwritten limitations into claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board may not import extra requirements that are not recited in the claim; courts will reverse where the Board imposes an unrecited limitation (citing In re Zletz). Example in opinion: Board's implicit requirement of user 'interaction' with a delivered 'list of goods' was an unwritten limitation not present in the claim language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intrinsic evidence controls claim scope (specification can define terms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim terms are interpreted in light of the specification; if the specification expressly defines a term (e.g., 'object' may include intangible items), that meaning can be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mapping a claim term to prior-art elements must be consistent with the patent specification; the opinion points out the specification explicitly stating that 'object' may be intangible (e.g., electronic music file), supporting mapping content promoted by a billboard to the claimed 'object.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency in construing related claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that share limitations should be construed consistently; dependent claims should not be given more stringent, unwritten requirements than their independent claim counterpart absent justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board construed claim 1 without requiring user 'interaction,' yet applied an 'interaction' requirement to dependent claims 37 and 43—an inconsistent and improper added limitation leading to reversal in the opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speculation is insufficient to meet prior-art disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Board conclusions that rely on speculation (e.g., that advertised products 'may be' in store vs. out of stock) are insufficient to show that prior art discloses a claim limitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factual findings must be grounded in evidence, not conjecture; where the Board labels an asserted mapping as 'speculation,' that rationale is inadequate to deny a finding of disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due process / APA notice requirement in IPRs
rubrics_metrics.description: Compliance with the APA and due process requires that a patent owner receive 'adequate notice of the issues that would be considered, and ultimately resolved, at that hearing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critical question is whether the patent owner had notice and opportunity to respond to an asserted mapping or theory; the opinion cites Genzyme and Pub. Serv. Comm'n of Ky. v. FERC. Example: raising a mapping at institution or oral argument and allowing sur-replies satisfies notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remand when Board fails to analyze subsequent limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: When the Board fails to analyze subsequent claim limitations (or otherwise errs such that not all limitations were considered), the proper remedy is vacatur and remand for the Board to consider the remaining limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the Board applied an incorrect legal standard or omitted analysis of later limitations, the Federal Circuit vacates and remands (opinion vacated Board's decision on claim 25 and dependent claims and remanded to consider subsequent limitations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversal appropriate where facts undisputed and Board committed analytical/legal errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Reversal is appropriate where 'the facts are largely undisputed, and the Board’s decision ... was mainly the result of the analytical errors.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court may reverse rather than remand when the record establishes the outcome under correct legal analysis (citing Smith & Nephew v. Rea).
